title: Magnitude-type mix accounted for most of a larger-event share decline in a 30-day Puerto Rico catalog sample
abstract: We tested whether a change in reported magnitude types accounts for a change in the share of larger earthquakes. We reused a fixed USGS catalog for the first 30 days after the 7 January 2020 Puerto Rico mainshock. Within 50 km, we compared days 1-7 with days 7-30. Among events of magnitude 2.5 or more, the share at magnitude 3.5 or more fell from 16.54% (106/641) to 8.35% (92/1102). A symmetric decomposition assigned -7.24 of the -8.19 percentage-point change to magnitude-type mix, and -0.95 points to change within types. With fixed pooled type weights, the change was -0.99 points. Its conditional 95% two-day block interval was -3.70 to 1.55 points. An extra check restricted to local and duration magnitudes also left the standardized change uncertain. This is a descriptive catalog result. Type choice depends on event properties and reporting practice. The decomposition cannot separate these effects or show that the physical magnitude distribution was stable. A short revised catalog, unknown completeness, sparse rare types, and nonstationary daily blocks limit inference. Code, exact input bytes, provenance, all checks, resample results and a figure are included.

display.caption: Left: larger-event shares by reported magnitude type. Right: the observed change, its two exact decomposition terms, and the change with fixed pooled weights. Intervals use daily blocks. Component intervals are conditional on all type groups being present in both resampled periods.
